abstract: "Psychologists increasingly report the probability of direction ($pd$), the posterior probability that a parameter lies on the side of the null value favored by the posterior, and claim a direction when $pd$ reaches a fixed threshold such as .975. Applied to many parameters, this rule produces more wrong claims as tests accumulate. We present an adjustment based on the classical Bayesian response to multiplicity, a penalty on the prior odds of each claim. Because the claimed direction is known only after the data, the penalty must cover both directions, so the researcher sets in advance $\\bar{\\pi}$, an upper bound on the prior probability of each direction, the same for every parameter in the family. A claim is made only if its posterior probability still reaches the threshold when its direction receives prior probability $1 - \\bar{\\pi}$. The adjustment uses only the $pd$ values and holds whenever the priors used to fit the model are continuous and symmetric about the null value. Because a directional claim about a null effect is false, the proportion of effects in the family that could be null offers a reference value for $\\bar{\\pi}$. Simulations show how the false discovery rate, the family-wise error rate, and power depend on $\\bar{\\pi}$, set below, at, or above the proportion of null effects. We also compare the rule with two alternative procedures, joint directional statements and simultaneous credible intervals. All three are implemented in the accompanying R package *multibayes*."

Over the past two decades, the use of Bayesian methods in psychological research has grown considerably [@Van2017; @Jevremov2024; @Pfadt2025]. This expansion has, however, been accompanied by practices reminiscent of the "null ritual" in frequentist statistics, where widespread adoption gave way to automatic application rather than principled reasoning [@Gigerenzer2004; @Cohen1994]. Researchers sometimes treat Bayes factor thresholds (e.g., BF > 3) as dichotomous decision rules, or claim that an effect "exists" because the posterior probability of a directional effect exceeds a conventional benchmark such as .975 [@Heck2023; @Kelter2023; @Tendeiro2024; @Hoijtink2016; @Tendeiro2019; @Kruschke2018]. Such cutoffs are convenient, but they encourage all-or-none interpretations. Moreover, when the same cutoff is applied to parameter after parameter, the resulting decisions face the multiplicity problem long recognized in frequentist statistics.

Frequentists developed methods to address this problem, controlling either the Family-Wise Error Rate (FWER; the probability of at least one false positive) or the False Discovery Rate (FDR; the expected proportion of false positives among rejected hypotheses) [@Benjamini1995; @Westfall1993]. These procedures address whether a spurious result enters the literature, but leave unresolved a subtler consequence of the same selection process. When researchers examine many parameters but highlight only the most extreme estimates, selection systematically inflates reported magnitudes [@Gelman2014; @Zwet2021; @Altoe2020]. Bayesian methods can mitigate this overestimation, pulling extreme estimates toward more plausible values through informative priors [@Zwet2022; @Dawid1994] and hierarchical modeling [@Gelman2012; @GelmanBook; @Kruschke2011; @Berry1999]. Magnitude bias and false-positive accumulation are, however, distinct problems. Shrinkage offers no guarantee about the error properties of a decision rule applied across many parameters: if the same cutoff is used repeatedly (e.g., claiming an effect whenever a posterior probability exceeds .975), the probability of spurious findings can remain substantial. Bayesian responses to this issue do exist, such as joint probability statements [@Gelman2000; @Pruzek2016; @Schnell2020; @Box1992] or priors over the hypothesis space that scale with the number of tests [@Scott2006; @Scott2010; @Jeffreys1938; @Westfall1997].

Here we focus on a decision rule based on the probability of direction ($pd$), which is increasingly used in psychological research [@Stone2024; @Brissenden2023; @Hochman2025; @Makowski2020; @Brissenden2024; @Ciranka2026; @Schurr2024; @Ben2022; @Bramley2022]. The $pd$ is the posterior probability that a parameter lies in its dominant direction [@Makowski2019; @Shi2021], and a direction is claimed when $pd$ exceeds a fixed threshold (e.g., $.95$ or $.975$). We examine the frequentist operating characteristics^[Although frequentist and Bayesian frameworks rest on different foundations, examining the frequentist operating characteristics of a Bayesian procedure (how it behaves over repeated use) is a well-established practice [@Zhang2019; @Ventz2015; @Müller2004].] of this rule and address the resulting multiplicity problem with the second strategy noted above, a penalty on the prior odds of each claim. This penalty is the classical Bayesian response to multiplicity, introduced by @Jeffreys1938 and developed by @Westfall1997, and it underlies more recent Bayesian approaches to FDR control [@Scott2006; @Scott2010; @Guo2010; @Abraham2022; @Efron2001; @Storey2003; @Storey2002] as well as the post hoc correction implemented in JASP [@Bergh2020; @deJong2019].

To our knowledge, the penalty has not been applied to $pd$. The obstacle is that the direction of a claim based on $pd$ is chosen by the data, so the penalty cannot be attached to a direction fixed in advance. Following robust Bayesian analysis [@Berger1994], we therefore consider a set of priors that lower the prior odds of either direction, and accept a claim only if it holds under all of them, that is, if its posterior probability under the prior most skeptical of it reaches the usual threshold. The size of the penalty is set by a single number chosen by the researcher, $\bar{\pi}$, an upper bound on the prior probability of each direction of a parameter. If no parameter in the family is judged more likely than another to lie above or below the null value, the same $\bar{\pi}$ applies to all of them. Its value expresses how skeptical the researcher is of a directional claim before the data. Because a directional claim about a null effect is false, the proportion of effects in the family that could be null offers a reference value for $\bar{\pi}$.

The paper proceeds as follows. We first introduce $pd$ and the rule based on it, and show why the rule produces more false directional claims as the number of tests grows. We then derive the adjustment, which needs only the $pd$ values, and discuss how to choose $\bar{\pi}$. A simulation study then shows how the FDR, the FWER, and power depend on $\bar{\pi}$, including values below and above the actual proportion of null effects, and compares the rule with joint directional statements and simultaneous credible intervals. Finally, we illustrate with a worked example the R package `multibayes`, which implements all three procedures, and conclude with a general discussion.

# Probability of Direction

The probability of direction ($pd$) is a posterior summary that quantifies how strongly the posterior distribution favors one direction of a parameter $\theta$ relative to a reference value $\theta_{\text{null}}$ [@Makowski2019]. For a continuous posterior, it can be defined as the larger of the two one-sided posterior probabilities, $pd = \max(\Pr(\theta < \theta_{\text{null}} \mid y),\ \Pr(\theta > \theta_{\text{null}} \mid y))$, and it ranges from .5 (no directional preference) to 1 (all on one side). The $pd$ equals exactly the complement of the one-sided $p$-value when computed on the posterior of a location parameter in exponential-family models estimated under a uniform prior; under a broader class of priors, this correspondence holds approximately [@Marsman2017; @Casella1987; @Shi2021]. For ease of exposition, we set $\theta_{\text{null}} = 0$ throughout; it can take any other value, which is particularly relevant when hypotheses involve a minimum effect of practical interest.

In practice, $pd$ is often used to summarize both the direction and the existence of an effect. This use is clearest when phrased as a decision rule, $pd \geq c$, which requires the posterior to assign at least $c$ probability mass to the side of $0$ it favors. Setting $c = 1 - \alpha/2$ is convenient because it bounds the posterior mass on the other side of $0$ by $\alpha/2$. For concreteness, suppose the posterior favors positive values, so that $pd = \Pr(\theta > 0 \mid y)$. With $\alpha = .05$, $c = .975$, and the rule requires $\Pr(\theta \le 0 \mid y) \leq .025$. The rule $pd \geq .975$ is therefore the same as the common practice of claiming an effect when the central 95% equal-tailed credible interval does not extend past $0$ (@fig-pd-ci), which is often read as showing that $0$ is relatively implausible [@Box1992]. Like the reference value of $0$, the threshold $c = .975$ is chosen only for ease of exposition, and any other posterior probability cutoff can be used.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pd-ci
#| fig-cap: "The Probability of Direction and the 95% Credible Interval"
#| apa-note: >
#|   Two normal posteriors for a parameter $\theta$, with the posterior mass below $0$ in orange and above $0$ in blue; the black bar is the central 95% equal-tailed credible interval. Panel A: $pd \geq .975$, and the interval does not extend past $0$. Panel B: $pd < .975$, and the interval includes $0$.
#| fig-width: 10.2
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# one panel: normal posterior with mean mu and sd s, shaded by side of 0
pd_ci_plot <- function(mu, s, tag) {
  x  <- seq(-1, 1, length.out = 2001)
  d  <- data.frame(x = x, y = dnorm(x, mu, s), side = ifelse(x > 0, "pos", "neg"))
  ci <- qnorm(c(0.025, 0.975), mu, s)
  p_pos <- 1 - pnorm(0, mu, s)
  # plotmath labels, one per line, so theta is drawn as a symbol
  lab <- c(sprintf('Pr(theta > 0 ~ "|" ~ italic(y)) == "%s"', nz(p_pos, 3)),
           sprintf('Pr(theta < 0 ~ "|" ~ italic(y)) == "%s"', nz(1 - p_pos, 3)),
           sprintf('italic(pd) == "%s"', nz(max(p_pos, 1 - p_pos), 3)),
           sprintf('"95%% CI = [%.2f, %.2f]"', ci[1], ci[2]))
  ggplot(d, aes(x, y)) +
    geom_area(aes(fill = side), show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey40") +
    annotate("segment", x = ci[1], xend = ci[2], y = 0, yend = 0, linewidth = 2.5, lineend = "round") +
    annotate("rect", xmin = -1, xmax = -0.1, ymin = 1.2, ymax = 2.45, fill = "white", colour = "grey30") +
    annotate("text", x = -0.96, y = c(2.25, 1.95, 1.65, 1.35), label = lab, parse = TRUE, hjust = 0, size = 4.2) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(neg = "#F8A31B", pos = "deepskyblue3")) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-0.5, 0, 0.5, 1)) +
    labs(x = expression(theta), y = "Posterior density", title = tag) +
    theme_clean(14) + theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
}
pd_ci_plot(0.35, 0.16, "A") | pd_ci_plot(0.30, 0.16, "B")
```

How often the rule $pd \geq c$ claims a direction when $\theta = 0$ depends on how $pd$ varies across repeated samples, and hence on the model and the prior. All illustrations and simulations use the normal model, as a representative case of parameters whose posterior is approximately normal. For a parameter $\theta$, $n$ independent observations are drawn from $\mathcal{N}(\theta, 1)$, and $\theta$ has the prior $\mathcal{N}(0, \tau)$, where $\tau$ is the prior standard deviation, so that the posterior of $\theta$ is also normal. Small values of $\tau$ give a narrow prior, concentrated near $0$, and large values a diffuse one. 

In this model, for a null effect ($\theta = 0$) under a diffuse prior, $pd$ is approximately uniform on $[.5, 1]$ across repeated samples (@fig-uniform-pd, $\tau = 2$). The rule $pd \geq c$ with $c = 1 - \alpha/2$ therefore claims a direction with probability about $\alpha$. A narrow prior shrinks $pd$ toward $.5$ and lowers this probability (@fig-uniform-pd, $\tau = 0.2$), but only for each test separately. With any fixed prior, the probability that at least one of $pd_1, \dots, pd_m$ reaches $c$ still grows with the number of tests $m$. For $m = 10$ independent tests of null effects with $n = 50$, for example, it is about $`r nz(fwer_null(10, 50, 2), 2)`$ under the diffuse prior and $`r nz(fwer_null(10, 50, 0.2), 2)`$ under the narrow one.


```{r}
#| label: fig-uniform-pd
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of the Probability of Direction Under the Null"
#| apa-note: >
#|   Density of $pd$ across repeated samples when $\theta = 0$, for observations $y_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\theta, 1)$ and a normal prior $\theta \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \tau)$, by sample size $n$ (rows) and prior standard deviation $\tau$ (columns). With a diffuse prior ($\tau = 2$), $pd$ is approximately uniform on $[.5, 1]$; a narrow prior ($\tau = 0.2$) shrinks it toward $.5$, especially in small samples. Bin width = 0.025.
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-width: 9
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Distribution function of pd under the null in the conjugate normal-normal model
pd_cdf <- function(p, n, tau) {
  s <- sqrt((n * tau^2) / (1 + n * tau^2))
  2 * pnorm(qnorm(p) / s) - 1
}
bin_width <- 0.025
breaks_pd <- seq(0.5, 1, by = bin_width)
grid_pd <- expand.grid(lower = breaks_pd[-length(breaks_pd)],
                       n = c(30, 50, 100), tau = c(0.2, 0.5, 2)) |>
  mutate(upper   = lower + bin_width,
         mid     = lower + bin_width / 2,
         density = (pd_cdf(upper, n, tau) - pd_cdf(lower, n, tau)) / bin_width,
         n_lab   = factor(sprintf("italic(n) == %d", n),
                          levels = sprintf("italic(n) == %d", c(30, 50, 100))),
         tau_lab = factor(sprintf("tau == %s", tau),
                          levels = sprintf("tau == %s", c(0.2, 0.5, 2))))

ggplot(grid_pd, aes(x = mid, y = density)) +
  geom_col(width = bin_width * 0.9, fill = "#F5A623", color = NA) +
  facet_grid(n_lab ~ tau_lab, labeller = label_parsed) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0.5, 1, by = 0.1)) +
  labs(x = expression(italic(pd)), y = "Density") +
  theme_clean(base_size = 14)
```

# Penalizing the Prior Odds of a Directional Claim

To limit the false claims that accumulate across tests, we penalize the prior odds of each directional claim, following @Jeffreys1938 and @Westfall1997.

## From the Probability of Direction to the Bayes Factor

As in the previous section, suppose that the posterior favors positive values. The claim is then that $\theta > 0$, which we denote $H_{+}$, and the opposite direction, $\theta < 0$, we denote $H_{-}$. We call the prior on $\theta$ specified in the fitted model the *estimation prior*, because the parameters are estimated under it. We assume that it is continuous and symmetric about $0$, as are normal or Student-$t$ priors centered on $0$ and, as a limit, flat priors. Symmetry makes $H_{+}$ and  $H_{-}$ equally probable a priori, $\Pr(H_{+}) = \Pr(H_{-}) = .5$, and after the data $pd = \Pr(H_{+} \mid y)$ and $1 - pd = \Pr(H_{-} \mid y)$.

The ratio $pd/(1 - pd)$ is therefore the posterior odds of $H_{+}$ against $H_{-}$, that is, how many times more probable $H_{+}$ is than $H_{-}$ after the data. By Bayes' rule, the posterior odds are the product of two terms,
$$
\frac{\Pr(H_{+} \mid y)}{\Pr(H_{-} \mid y)} = \text{BF}_{+-} \times \frac{\Pr(H_{+})}{\Pr(H_{-})}.
$$
The second term, the prior odds, says how many times more probable $H_{+}$ is than $H_{-}$ before the data. The first, the Bayes factor $\text{BF}_{+-}$, says by how much the data change these odds. Under the symmetric estimation prior, the prior odds are $.5/.5 = 1$, so the posterior odds equal the Bayes factor [@Marsman2017],
$$
\frac{pd}{1 - pd} = \text{BF}_{+-}.
$$
For a parameter with $pd = .988$, for example, $\text{BF}_{+-} = .988/.012 \approx 82$, so the data are about 82 times more probable under $H_{+}$ than under $H_{-}$.

The rule $pd \geq c$ can thus be written as a rule on the Bayes factor. Because the odds $pd/(1 - pd)$ increase with $pd$,
$$
pd \geq c \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \frac{pd}{1 - pd} \geq \frac{c}{1 - c} \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \text{BF}_{+-} \geq \frac{c}{1 - c}.
$$
With $c = .975$, a direction is claimed whenever the Bayes factor is at least $.975/.025 = 39$. Because the prior odds are fixed at one, the Bayes factor alone decides every claim.

## Prior Odds With Many Tests

Consider now a family of $m$ tests, indexed by $i = 1, \dots, m$, each concerning a parameter $\theta_i$ with probability of direction $pd_i$. Under the symmetric estimation prior, each parameter is equally likely to be positive or negative before the data. Whichever direction is later claimed, the claim is therefore false with prior probability $.5$. If the parameters are independent a priori, the prior probability that all $m$ claims are false, an event we denote $H_0$, is the product of these probabilities, $.5^m$. With $m = 5$, $\Pr(H_0) = .5^{5} \approx .03$, so before any data the estimation prior gives probability $1 - .03 = .97$ to at least one claim in the family being correct. This probability approaches one as more parameters are tested. Yet the threshold $c$ states how much posterior probability a single claim requires, and the rule $pd \geq c$ applies it to every parameter as if it were the only one tested.

The classical response to this problem is to lower the prior odds of each claim, to reflect that many parameters are tested. Suppose first that the direction of a parameter is predicted before the data, say $\theta > 0$. The researcher then gives the opposite direction, $H_{-}$, a prior probability $\pi$ larger than $.5$, and $H_{+}$ the probability $1 - \pi$, so the prior odds of $H_{+}$ become $(1 - \pi)/\pi$, below one.

The prior odds can be lowered without changing the shape of the estimation prior on either side of $0$. For the prior $\mathcal{N}(0, \tau)$ of the normal model, let $\mathcal{N}_{-}(0, \tau)$ and $\mathcal{N}_{+}(0, \tau)$ denote this normal truncated to negative and to positive values, so that the estimation prior is $.5\,\mathcal{N}_{-} + .5\,\mathcal{N}_{+}$. The reweighted prior
$$
\pi\,\mathcal{N}_{-}(0, \tau) + (1 - \pi)\,\mathcal{N}_{+}(0, \tau)
$$
moves probability from the positive to the negative side and keeps the shape within each side. The likelihood averaged over each side, and hence the Bayes factor $pd/(1 - pd)$, is the same as under the estimation prior. Only the prior odds change, and the posterior odds of $H_{+}$ become 
$$\text{BF}_{+-} \times \frac{1 - \pi}{\pi}.$$

The remaining question is how large $\pi$ should be. @Jeffreys1938 and @Westfall1997 fixed the prior probability of $H_0$ in advance, at the same value whatever the size of the family. With the penalty, $\Pr(H_0) = \pi^m$ for independent parameters, so keeping $\Pr(H_0)$ fixed requires $\pi$ to grow with $m$. Fixing $\Pr(H_0) = .5$, for example, makes the event that all claims are false and the event that at least one claim is correct equally probable before the data, and gives $\pi = .5^{1/m}$, which is $`r nz(.5^(1/2), 2)`$ for $m = 2$, $`r nz(.5^(1/5), 2)`$ for $m = 5$, and $`r nz(.5^(1/20), 2)`$ for $m = 20$. A larger $\pi$ gives smaller prior odds, so the Bayes factor needed for a claim grows with $m$, much as the per-test threshold does in the frequentist Bonferroni correction [@Westfall1997].


## A Set of Priors Penalizing Either Direction

With $pd$, however, the direction to be claimed is not known before the data, because it is the side the posterior favors. We therefore apply the penalty of the previous section to each direction in turn. With $\pi = .8$, for example, this gives two reweighted versions of the estimation prior, one that gives $\theta < 0$ probability $.8$ and so penalizes the claim $\theta > 0$, and one that gives $\theta > 0$ probability $.8$ and so penalizes the claim $\theta < 0$. The value $.8$ is treated as an upper bound, so every prior in between is also allowed, including the estimation prior with $.5$ on each side.

In general, the researcher fixes before the data an upper bound $\bar{\pi}$, between $.5$ and $1$. The class $\Gamma$, the set of priors considered, contains every prior obtained by reweighting the two halves of the estimation prior so that each side of $0$ has prior probability between $1 - \bar{\pi}$ and $\bar{\pi}$ (@fig-class shows the class for $\bar{\pi} = .7$ and $\bar{\pi} = .9$). With $\bar{\pi} = .5$, the estimation prior is the only prior in $\Gamma$, and no penalty is applied.

```{r}
#| label: fig-class
#| fig-cap: "The Class of Priors for Two Values of $\\bar{\\pi}$"
#| apa-note: >

Panel A: for $\bar{\pi} = .7$, the prior probability of $\theta > 0$ lies between $.3$ and $.7$; the colored lines are the two extreme priors of the class, the one most skeptical of $\theta > 0$ (solid) and the one most skeptical of $\theta < 0$ (dashed). Panel B: the same for $\bar{\pi} = .9$, for which the prior probability of $\theta > 0$ lies between $.1$ and $.9$. A larger $\bar{\pi}$ gives a wider class.
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-pos: htbp
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

c_ex <- 0.975
w_a <- function(x, a) ifelse(x > 0, 2 * a, 2 * (1 - a))
ttl <- theme(legend.position = "top", plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

# the estimation prior and the two extreme priors of the class, for a given pi0
lab3  <- c("mid", "low", "high")
labx  <- c("Estimation prior",
           expression("Most skeptical of " * theta > 0),
           expression("Most skeptical of " * theta < 0))
cols3 <- c(mid = "black", low = "#F8A31B", high = "deepskyblue3")
ltys3 <- c(mid = "solid", low = "solid", high = "dashed")
xa <- seq(-3, 3, length.out = 2001); pa0 <- dnorm(xa)
class_plot <- function(p0, tag) {
  dA <- data.frame(theta = rep(xa, 3),
                   dens  = c(pa0, pa0 * w_a(xa, 1 - p0), pa0 * w_a(xa, p0)),
                   prior = factor(rep(lab3, each = length(xa)), levels = lab3))
  band <- data.frame(theta = xa, lo = pa0 * 2 * (1 - p0), hi = pa0 * 2 * p0)
  ggplot() +
    geom_ribbon(data = band, aes(theta, ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "grey85") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey40") +
    geom_line(data = dA, aes(theta, dens, colour = prior, linetype = prior), linewidth = 1.1) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = cols3, labels = labx) +
    scale_linetype_manual(values = ltys3, labels = labx) +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 2 * 0.9 * dnorm(0))) +
    labs(x = expression(theta), y = "Prior density", colour = NULL, linetype = NULL,
         title = bquote(bold(.(tag))*"   "*bar(pi) == .(sub("^0", "", format(p0))))) +
    theme_clean(15) + ttl
}
(class_plot(0.7, "A") | class_plot(0.9, "B")) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") & theme(legend.position = "top")
```

A claim about $\theta_i$ is made only if its posterior probability is at least $c$ under every prior in $\Gamma$. As in the previous section, these priors share the Bayes factor and differ only in the prior odds, so this probability is smallest under the prior that gives the claimed direction the lowest prior probability, $1 - \bar{\pi}$ (solid line in @fig-class for the claim $\theta > 0$). We call it the prior most skeptical of the claim. Under this prior, the posterior odds of the claim are those of the previous section with $\bar{\pi}$ in place of $\pi$, and the corresponding probability is
$$
pd_{\text{adj},i} = \frac{pd_i\,(1 - \bar{\pi})}{pd_i\,(1 - \bar{\pi}) + (1 - pd_i)\,\bar{\pi}}.
$$
A claim is made when $pd_{\text{adj},i} \geq c$, with the same threshold $c$ as before. Since $pd_{\text{adj},i}$ increases with $pd_i$, this requires $pd_i$ to reach the value
$$
c^* = \frac{c\,\bar{\pi}}{(1 - c)(1 - \bar{\pi}) + c\,\bar{\pi}}.
$$
With $c = .975$ and $\bar{\pi} = .8$, $c^* = `r nz(.975 * .8 / (.025 * .2 + .975 * .8), 4)`$. The adjustment is therefore equivalent to raising the threshold on $pd$ from $c$ to $c^*$. Since $\Gamma$ is fixed before the data, the data decide only which direction is claimed, and hence which prior in $\Gamma$ is the most skeptical.

Unlike $pd$, which is at least $.5$ by definition, $pd_{\text{adj}}$ can fall below $.5$. Take a parameter with $pd = .7$, favoring $\theta > 0$, and $\bar{\pi} = .8$. Its Bayes factor is $.7/.3 \approx 2.3$. Under the prior most skeptical of $\theta > 0$, the prior odds of $\theta > 0$ are $.25$ ($.2/.8$), so its posterior odds are $2.3 \times .25 \approx .58$ and $pd_{\text{adj}} \approx .37$. Under the prior most skeptical of $\theta < 0$, the prior odds of $\theta > 0$ are $4$ instead ($.8/.2$), and its posterior probability is about $.90$. The priors in $\Gamma$ thus disagree on which direction is more probable. A value of $pd_{\text{adj}}$ below $.5$ does not mean that the data favor the opposite direction. It means that, with the skepticism allowed by $\bar{\pi}$, the data do not establish even which direction is more probable. In general, $pd_{\text{adj}}$ falls below $.5$ whenever $pd < \bar{\pi}$.

@fig-rule, Panel A, illustrates the rule for $\bar{\pi} = .7$, for which $c^* = .989$. Each bar spans the posterior probability of $\theta > 0$ across $\Gamma$, and its left end is $pd_{\text{adj}}$. A parameter with $pd = .980$ exceeds $c = .975$ under the estimation prior but not under every prior in $\Gamma$ ($pd_{\text{adj}} = `r nz(.98 * .3 / (.98 * .3 + .02 * .7), 3)`$), so no claim is made, whereas parameters with $pd = .990$ and $pd = .999$ are claimed. With $\bar{\pi} = .9$ (Panel B), the class is wider (@fig-class, Panel B), and $c^* = `r nz(.975 * .9 / (.025 * .1 + .975 * .9), 3)`$, so only the parameter with $pd = .999$ is claimed.

```{r}
#| label: fig-rule
#| dependson: fig-class
#| fig-cap: "The Resulting Rule for Two Values of $\\bar{\\pi}$"
#| apa-note: >
#|   For four parameters, the range of the posterior probability of $\theta > 0$ across $\Gamma$ (bars), whose left end is $pd_{\text{adj}}$, and its value under the estimation prior, $pd$ (circles). A claim is made only when the whole bar lies at or above $c = .975$ (dashed line), that is, when $pd_{\text{adj}} \geq c$, which is equivalent to $pd \geq c^*$. Panel A: for $\bar{\pi} = .7$, $c^* = .989$. Panel B: for $\bar{\pi} = .9$, $c^* = .997$. A larger $\bar{\pi}$ gives a wider class and longer bars, so fewer parameters are claimed; note the different scales of the x-axes.
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# range of Pr(theta > 0 | y) over the class, one bar per parameter, for a given pi0
post_a <- function(pd, a) pd * a / (pd * a + (1 - pd) * (1 - a))
pds <- c(0.97, 0.98, 0.99, 0.999)
rule_plot <- function(p0, tag, xmin, xby) {
  dB <- data.frame(eff = factor(sprintf("%.3f", pds), levels = sprintf("%.3f", rev(pds))),
                   lo = post_a(pds, 1 - p0), mid = pds, hi = post_a(pds, p0))
  dB$claim <- factor(ifelse(dB$lo >= c_ex, "claimed", "not claimed"), levels = c("claimed", "not claimed"))
  ggplot(dB, aes(y = eff)) +
    geom_segment(aes(x = lo, xend = hi, yend = eff, colour = claim), linewidth = 3.2, lineend = "round") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = c_ex, linetype = "dashed") +
    annotate("text", x = c_ex, y = 4.45, label = "italic(c) == 0.975", parse = TRUE, hjust = 1.08, size = 4) +
    geom_point(aes(x = mid), shape = 21, fill = "white", size = 3, stroke = 1.1) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c("claimed" = "black", "not claimed" = "grey70"), name = NULL, drop = FALSE) +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(xmin, 1), breaks = seq(1, xmin, -xby)) +
    labs(x = expression(Pr(theta > 0 ~ "|" ~ italic(y)) ~ "across the class"),
         y = expression(italic(pd)),
         title = bquote(bold(.(tag))*"   "*bar(pi) == .(sub("^0", "", format(p0))))) +
    theme_clean(15) + ttl + theme(axis.text.y = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 1), axis.title.y = element_text(angle = 0, vjust = 0.5))
}
(rule_plot(0.7, "A", 0.925, 0.01) | rule_plot(0.9, "B", 0.75, 0.05)) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") & theme(legend.position = "top")
```

## What $\bar{\pi}$ Means and How to Choose It

The bound $\bar{\pi}$ says how skeptical the researcher is of a directional claim before the data. Under the prior in $\Gamma$ most skeptical of a claim, the claimed direction has prior probability $1 - \bar{\pi}$ and the opposite direction $\bar{\pi}$. With $\bar{\pi} = .5$ there is no penalty, and with $\bar{\pi} = .8$ a claim needs a Bayes factor four times larger than without the adjustment. We use the same $\bar{\pi}$ for every parameter in a family. This requires the parameters to be exchangeable in direction, that is, no parameter is judged more likely than another to lie on a given side of $0$. Every prior in $\Gamma$ gives each direction a prior probability between $1 - \bar{\pi}$ and $\bar{\pi}$, and for exchangeable parameters this range is also the range of the expected proportion of parameters in the family lying in that direction.

Through this proportion, null effects can guide the choice of $\bar{\pi}$. If up to 70% of the effects in a family could be null, at most 30% lie in each direction. The class should then allow each direction a prior probability as low as $.3$, which gives $\bar{\pi} = .7$. This choice concerns both directions and is made before the data. The proportion of effects that could be null is thus a reference value for $\bar{\pi}$, and larger values give fewer false claims. Because the priors in $\Gamma$ give no probability to $0$, the share of the null effects goes to the opposite direction, not to $0$. $pd_{\text{adj}}$ therefore remains the posterior probability of a sign, and $1 - c$ bounds the probability that a claim has the wrong sign.

This skepticism cannot be built into the estimation prior. However narrow, a symmetric prior gives each direction prior probability $.5$, so it cannot lower the prior odds of a claim. A narrower prior makes claims rarer only by pulling every estimate toward $0$, which changes what the prior says about the size of the parameters. The adjustment leaves the estimation prior to describe the plausible sizes of each parameter and to give the estimates, and expresses the skepticism through $\bar{\pi}$ alone. Because the sign of a parameter does not depend on its unit, the estimation priors can differ across parameters, for example when one effect is a slope per year of age and another a difference between groups, as long as the same skepticism about direction applies to all of them.

For independent parameters, $\bar{\pi}$ can also be set through a fixed $\Pr(H_0)$ instead of the proportion of null effects, as in @Jeffreys1938 and @Westfall1997. The proportion of null effects keeps $\bar{\pi}$ the same whatever the size of the family, which suits the aim of keeping the proportion of false claims low. A fixed $\Pr(H_0)$ makes $\bar{\pi}$ grow with the size of the family, which suits the aim of avoiding any false claim.

# Simulation Study

## Design

We simulated families of $m$ parameters, a proportion $\pi_0$ of which were null effects ($\theta_i = 0$), and applied the rule $pd_{\text{adj}} \geq c$, with $c = .975$, for several values of $\bar{\pi}$. Four factors were fully crossed, with 10,000 replications per condition. The bound $\bar{\pi}$ took the values $.5, .6, \dots, .9$, where $\bar{\pi} = .5$ is the unadjusted rule; the proportion of null effects $\pi_0$ took the values $.5, .6, \dots, 1$; the family size $m$ was 4, 8, 10, or 20; and the sample size $n$ was 30, 50, or 100. In each replication, the number of null effects was drawn from $\mathrm{Binomial}(m, \pi_0)$, and the remaining parameters were set to $\theta_i = 0.3$. Data and posteriors followed the conjugate normal-normal model described in the section on $pd$, with $n$ observations per parameter and a diffuse prior ($\tau = 2$), so that $pd$ was computed exactly from the normal posterior. 

For each family, let $R$ be the total number of claims and $V$ the number of false claims. Claims regarding null effects were false regardless of direction, whereas claims regarding an effect of 0.3 were false only if they asserted $\theta_i < 0$. We evaluated the FDR, $\mathbb{E}[V/\max(R, 1)]$ [@Benjamini1995; @Benjamini2005]; the FWER, $\Pr(V > 0)$; and average power, the proportion of non-null effects claimed in the correct direction. 

Here, $\bar{\pi}$ reflects the researcher's judgment and $\pi_0$ the actual proportion of null effects. We term $\bar{\pi} = \pi_0$ a matched value, the reference value described in the previous section. The probability of a wrong-sign claim for an effect of 0.3 was at most $.00015$, so nearly all false claims were claims about null effects. A setting of $\bar{\pi} < \pi_0$ underestimates the null proportion, while $\bar{\pi} > \pi_0$ is conservative.

## Error Rates and Power of the Prior-Odds Rule

```{r}
#| label: sim-numbers
#| include: false
# numbers reported in the text of this section
mt <- df_pi0 |> filter(near(pi0, pi0_true))      # matched pi.bar
fdr_unadj_max  <- max(df_pi0$FDR[near(df_pi0$pi0, 0.5)])
fdr_mt_min     <- min(mt$FDR)
fdr_mt_max     <- max(mt$FDR)
fdr_under      <- df_pi0 |> filter(m == 20, n == 50, near(pi0, 0.6), near(pi0_true, 0.9)) |> pull(FDR)
pw_unadj       <- df_pi0 |> filter(m == 20, n == 50, near(pi0, 0.5)) |> pull(pw) |> mean(na.rm = TRUE)
pw_90          <- df_pi0 |> filter(m == 20, n == 50, near(pi0, 0.9)) |> pull(pw) |> mean(na.rm = TRUE)
fwer_unadj_max <- max(df_pi0$FWER[df_pi0$n == 50 & near(df_pi0$pi0, 0.5)])
fwer_90_max    <- max(df_pi0$FWER[df_pi0$n == 50 & near(df_pi0$pi0, 0.9)])
fwer_h0_max    <- max(df_h0$FWER[df_h0$n == 50])
```

@fig-ind-fdr-pw, Panel A, shows the FDR. For the unadjusted rule (row $\bar{\pi} = .5$), the FDR grows with the family size and with $\pi_0$, and reaches $`r nz(fdr_unadj_max)`$ when $m = 20$ and all effects are null. With a matched $\bar{\pi}$ (outlined cells), it lies between $`r nz(fdr_mt_min)`$ and $`r nz(fdr_mt_max)`$ across all conditions, with the largest values in the largest families and smallest samples. The FDR is high only when $\bar{\pi}$ underestimates $\pi_0$ by a wide margin in a large family. With $m = 20$ and $n = 50$, for example, $\bar{\pi} = .6$ gives an FDR of $`r nz(fdr_under)`$ when $\pi_0 = .9$.

A lower FDR costs power (@fig-ind-fdr-pw, Panel B). Power depends on $\bar{\pi}$ and $n$, but not on $m$ or $\pi_0$, because $pd_{\text{adj}}$ depends only on the $pd$ of the parameter and on $\bar{\pi}$, not on the size of the family. Panel B therefore shows $m = 20$ only. With $n = 50$, for example, power falls from $`r nz(pw_unadj)`$ for the unadjusted rule to $`r nz(pw_90)`$ with $\bar{\pi} = .9$. 

```{r}

The row $\bar{\pi} = .5$ is the unadjusted rule, where the prior odds are one and $pd_{\text{adj}} = pd$; outlined cells mark matched values, $\bar{\pi} = \pi_0$. Each cell is the empirical FDR or power over 10,000 replications.

d_fdr <- df_pi0 |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    facet_m = factor(paste0("m = ", m), levels = paste0("m = ", sort(unique(m)))),
    facet_n = factor(paste0("n = ", n), levels = paste0("n = ", sort(unique(n)))))
fdr_heat <- ggplot(d_fdr, aes(x = factor(pi0_true), y = factor(pi0), fill = FDR)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(FDR, 2)), size = 8, color = "black", fontface = "bold") +
  # matched values: pi0 = pi0_true
  geom_tile(data = dplyr::filter(d_fdr, abs(pi0 - pi0_true) < 1e-9), fill = NA, colour = "black", linewidth = 1.9) +
  facet_grid(facet_m ~ facet_n) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(
    colours = c("green4", "#B8E186", "#FFFFBF", "#F4A582", "#B2182B"),
    values  = scales::rescale(c(0, 0.09, 0.15, 0.20, 0.7), from = c(0, 0.7)),
    limits  = c(0, 0.7), oob = scales::squish, na.value = "grey90",
    breaks  = c(0, 0.10, 0.20, 0.40, 0.7),
    labels  = scales::label_number(accuracy = 0.01), name = "FDR",
    guide   = guide_colorbar(barheight = unit(8, "cm"), barwidth = unit(1, "cm"),
                             title.position = "top", title.hjust = 0.5)) +
  labs(x = expression(italic(pi)[0]), y = expression(bar(italic(pi)))) +
  theme_clean(28) +
  theme(legend.position = "right", strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
        axis.text.y = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 1), axis.title.y = element_text(angle = 0, vjust = 0.5))

p_pw_heat <- df_pi0 |>
    filter(pi0_true != 1, m == 20) |>
    mutate(
      m = factor(m, levels = sort(unique(m))),
      facet_label_m = factor(paste0("m = ", m),
                             levels = paste0("m = ", sort(unique(m)))),
      n = factor(n, levels = sort(unique(n))),
      facet_label_n = factor(paste0("n = ", n),
                             levels = paste0("n = ", sort(unique(n))))) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = factor(pi0_true), y = factor(pi0),
               fill = pw)) +
    geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
    geom_text(aes(label = round(pw, 2)),
              size = 8, color = "black", fontface = "bold") +
    geom_tile(data = function(d) dplyr::filter(d, abs(pi0 - pi0_true) < 1e-9), fill = NA, colour = "black", linewidth = 1.9) +
    facet_grid(facet_label_m ~ facet_label_n) +
    scale_fill_gradientn(
    colours  = c("#B2182B", "#FFFFBF", "green4"),
    values   = scales::rescale(c(0, 0.5, 0.8), from = c(0, 0.8)),
    limits   = c(0, 0.8),
    oob      = scales::squish,
    na.value = "grey90"
  ) +
    labs(
  x = expression(italic(pi)[0]),
  y = expression(bar(italic(pi))),
  fill = "power"
)+theme_clean(28)+
    theme(legend.position = "right",
          strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
          axis.text.y = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 1), axis.title.y = element_text(angle = 0, vjust = 0.5))

(fdr_heat/p_pw_heat)+
  plot_layout(heights = c(4, 0.9))+

```

@fig-ind-fwer shows the FWER for $n = 50$, as a representative case. Because the rule for each parameter does not change with $m$, the FWER for a fixed $\bar{\pi}$ grows with the family size. It reaches $`r nz(fwer_unadj_max)`$ for the unadjusted rule when $m = 20$ and all effects are null, and stays at or below $`r nz(fwer_90_max)`$ with $\bar{\pi} = .9$. Setting $\bar{\pi}$ through a fixed $\Pr(H_0)$, which raises $\bar{\pi}$ with $m$, removes this growth. With $\Pr(H_0) = .5$ (top row of each panel), the FWER stays at or below $`r nz(fwer_h0_max)`$ for every family size.

## Comparison With Other Bayesian Methods

```{r}
#| label: compare-numbers
#| include: false
# numbers reported in the text of the comparison (n = 50)
load(file.path("script", "output", "df_compare.rda"))
c50     <- df_compare |> filter(n == 50)
band    <- c50 |> filter(method == "simultaneous")
mt50    <- c50 |> filter(method == "prior-odds", near(pi0, pi0_true))
joint20 <- c50 |> filter(method == "joint", m == 20)
fdr_joint_50  <- joint20$FDR[near(joint20$pi0_true, 0.5)]
fdr_joint_90  <- joint20$FDR[near(joint20$pi0_true, 0.9)]
fdr_joint_100 <- joint20$FDR[near(joint20$pi0_true, 1)]
# power lost by the joint rule relative to the unadjusted rule
loss <- c50 |> filter(method == "joint") |> dplyr::select(m, pi0_true, pw_joint = pw) |>
  left_join(c50 |> filter(method == "prior-odds", near(pi0, 0.5)) |> dplyr::select(m, pi0_true, pw_unadj = pw),
            by = c("m", "pi0_true"))
loss_4  <- max((loss$pw_unadj - loss$pw_joint)[loss$m == 4], na.rm = TRUE)
loss_20 <- max((loss$pw_unadj - loss$pw_joint)[loss$m == 20], na.rm = TRUE)
```

We compare the prior-odds rule with two Bayesian alternatives. The first, hereafter the *joint directional rule*, orders the directional claims by their posterior probability and accepts the largest set whose joint posterior probability is at least $c$ [@Gelman2000; @Pruzek2016]. It claims the direction favored by the posterior, and what it limits is the posterior probability that any of the accepted claims has the wrong sign. The second, hereafter the *simultaneous-band rule*, computes credible intervals such that the joint posterior probability that every interval contains its parameter equals a set value, and claims a direction for a parameter whenever its interval excludes 0 [@Schnell2020; @Schnell2016; @Box1992].

The two procedures were applied to the same replications as the prior-odds rule, using 10,000 draws from each posterior, and we report the results for $n = 50$, as a representative case. All three procedures used $c = .975$. The joint directional rule requires a joint posterior probability of at least $.975$, the simultaneous band has a joint posterior probability of $.95$, which for a single parameter is the 95% equal-tailed interval and so corresponds to $pd \geq .975$, and the prior-odds rule claims a direction when $pd_{\text{adj}} \geq .975$. @fig-compare shows their FDR, FWER, and power, together with those of the prior-odds rule with a matched $\bar{\pi}$ ($\bar{\pi} = \pi_0$).

The simultaneous-band rule keeps both error rates low in every condition. Its FWER ranges from $`r nz(min(band$FWER), 3)`$ to $`r nz(max(band$FWER), 3)`$, at or below $.05$ or within the Monte Carlo band around it in all conditions. The error rates of the joint directional rule, in contrast, increase with the proportion of null effects, and its FWER also with the family size. At $m = 20$, its FDR rises from $`r nz(fdr_joint_50)`$ at $\pi_0 = .5$ to $`r nz(fdr_joint_90)`$ at $\pi_0 = .9$ and $`r nz(fdr_joint_100)`$ when all effects are null. Its first claim requires the same $pd \geq .975$ as the unadjusted rule, and each further claim must keep the joint probability at or above $.975$, so it makes a subset of the unadjusted rule's claims. Its error rates are therefore lower than those of the unadjusted rule when some effects are non-null, and practically equal to them when all effects are null.

With a matched $\bar{\pi}$, the FDR of the prior-odds rule stays between $`r nz(min(mt50$FDR))`$ and $`r nz(max(mt50$FDR))`$, with the largest values at $m = 20$. It is thus much lower than that of the unadjusted rule, but not always at or below $.05$, because the rule is not built to guarantee a nominal level. Its FWER decreases as $\pi_0$ increases, because a matched $\bar{\pi}$ increases with it. 

Lower error rates come with lower power. The joint directional rule loses little power relative to the unadjusted rule, at most $`r nz(loss_4)`$ at $m = 4$ and $`r nz(loss_20)`$ at $m = 20$. The simultaneous band loses the most, and its power decreases with the family size. At $m = 20$ it has less power than the prior-odds rule with any $\bar{\pi}$. The power of the prior-odds rule does not depend on $m$, but on $\bar{\pi}$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-compare
#| fig-cap: "False Discovery Rate, Family-Wise Error Rate, and Power of the Three Procedures"
#| apa-note: >
#|   False Discovery Rate (FDR, top row), Family-Wise Error Rate (FWER, middle row), and average power (bottom row) as a function of the true proportion of null effects, $\pi_0$ (x-axis), by family size $m$ (columns), with $n = 50$. Blue squares show the prior-odds rule with a matched $\bar{\pi}$, $\bar{\pi} = \pi_0$, which stops at $\pi_0 = .9$ because with $\bar{\pi} = 1$ no claim would ever be made, orange circles the joint directional rule (joint posterior probability of at least $.975$), and grey triangles the simultaneous-band rule (simultaneous credible intervals with joint posterior probability $.95$). The dotted line marks $.05$, and the grey band around it its 95% Monte Carlo band, that is, $.046$ to $.054$. Panel A shows all rates on their full scale; Panel B shows the two error rates between 0 and .12, where the band is visible and points of the joint directional rule above .12 are cut off. Each point is the empirical rate over 10,000 replications.
#| fig-width: 21
#| fig-height: 21
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-align: left

d_cmp <- df_compare |>
  # n = 50; the prior-odds rule only with a matched pi0, which exists up to pi0_true = .9
  dplyr::filter(n == 50, method != "prior-odds" | abs(pi0 - pi0_true) < 1e-9) |>
  dplyr::select(method, m, pi0_true, FDR, FWER, power = pw) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(FDR, FWER, power), names_to = "metric", values_to = "rate") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    method  = factor(method, levels = c("prior-odds", "joint", "simultaneous")),
    metric  = factor(metric, levels = c("FDR", "FWER", "power"), labels = c("FDR", "FWER", "Power")),
    facet_m = factor(paste0("m = ", m), levels = paste0("m = ", sort(unique(m))))) |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(rate))   # power is undefined when every effect is null
# reference line at .05 for the two error rates, with its 95% Monte Carlo band
# (10,000 replications; for the FDR, a mean of values in [0, 1], the band is conservative)
ref05 <- data.frame(metric = factor(c("FDR", "FWER"), levels = levels(d_cmp$metric)), y = 0.05)
mc_half <- qnorm(0.975) * sqrt(0.05 * 0.95 / 1e4)
ref05$lo <- 0.05 - mc_half; ref05$hi <- 0.05 + mc_half
lab_proc <- c(expression("Prior-odds, "*bar(italic(pi)) == italic(pi)[0]), "Joint directional", "Simultaneous band")

# one panel of the comparison: rows are metrics, columns family sizes
cmp_plot <- function(d, ref, ylim = NULL) {
  ggplot(d, aes(x = pi0_true, y = rate, colour = method, shape = method)) +
    geom_rect(data = ref, aes(xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = lo, ymax = hi), inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = "grey85") +
    geom_hline(data = ref, aes(yintercept = y), colour = "grey50", linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 1) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1.6) +
    geom_point(size = 4.5) +
    facet_grid(metric ~ facet_m, scales = "free_y", switch = "y") +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = ylim) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c("#1F4E9C", "#F8A31B", "grey35"), labels = lab_proc, name = NULL) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c(15, 16, 17), labels = lab_proc, name = NULL) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0.5, 1, 0.1), labels = c(".5", ".6", ".7", ".8", ".9", "1")) +
    labs(x = expression(italic(pi)[0]), y = NULL) +
    theme_clean(28) +
    theme(strip.placement = "outside", strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
          legend.position = "bottom", legend.key.width = unit(2.5, "cm"),
          panel.spacing = unit(1, "cm"), axis.text.y = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 1), axis.title.y = element_text(angle = 0, vjust = 0.5))
}
# Panel A: all rates on their full scale; Panel B: the error rates near .05
p_full <- cmp_plot(d_cmp, ref05)
p_zoom <- cmp_plot(dplyr::filter(d_cmp, metric != "Power"), ref05, ylim = c(0, 0.12)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.05, 0.10), labels = c("0", ".05", ".10"))
(p_full / p_zoom) +
  plot_layout(heights = c(3, 2), guides = "collect") +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.tag = element_text(size = 34, face = "bold"))
```


The choice among the three procedures thus depends on the aim. If only a small proportion of false claims is acceptable (FDR), the prior-odds rule addresses this aim through $\bar{\pi}$, which only this rule asks the researcher to state. If any false claim must be avoided (FWER), the simultaneous band kept the FWER close to or below $.05$ in these simulations. The joint directional rule is applicable either when the prior accurately reflects the data-generating process [e.g., @Gelman2000] or when the selected subset is pre-specified and the overall pattern of predictions is evaluated as a single claim (e.g., theory predicts $\theta_1 > 0$ and $\theta_2 > 0$).

The three procedures also differ in the kind of statement they support about the set of claims. All three statements are posterior probabilities about the sign of the parameters, computed under continuous priors that give null effects no probability. None of them is therefore the FDR or the FWER of the simulations, which also count claims about null effects as false. Every claim made by the prior-odds rule has a posterior probability of at least $c$ under every prior in $\Gamma$, so it has the wrong sign with probability at most $1 - c$, and the expected proportion of claims with the wrong sign among those made is also at most $1 - c$, that is, $.025$ for $c = .975$. The rule does not give the probability that all the claims hold together, which can be lower, about $.975^3 \approx .93$ for three independent claims at $.975$. The other two procedures give this probability. The joint directional rule accepts a set of claims only if they hold together with a posterior probability of at least $.975$ under the estimation prior, so the probability that any of the accepted claims has the wrong sign is at most $.025$. This statement covers only the accepted subset, and it is made with prior odds of one for every direction, whereas the prior-odds rule lowers the prior odds of every claim in the family through $\bar{\pi}$. The simultaneous band gives a claim about each parameter whose interval excludes $0$, and because all intervals contain their parameters together with posterior probability $.95$, the claims made also hold together with at least that probability.


# Application: Worked Example With the R Package `multibayes`

The procedures are implemented in the `multibayes` R package. The function `pd.adjust()` accepts either a matrix of posterior draws, from which $pd$ values are computed internally, or a vector of pre-computed $pd$ values. The penalty is specified either directly as $\bar{\pi}$ (argument `pi.max`) or as $\Pr(H_0)$ (argument `p0`), from which $\bar{\pi} = \Pr(H_0)^{1/m}$. The threshold $c$, the posterior probability required to make a claim, is set with the argument `threshold` (default $.975$).

For this example, we use the openly available dataset from @Lin2020, who investigated the effect of ego depletion on conflict resolution across four studies. In their paradigm, an initial high-demand (vs. low-demand) task was followed by a Stroop task. For simplicity, we focus on Study 1, which tested the effects of congruency and ego depletion (within subjects). The dataset is readily accessible via the `afex` package [@Singmann2016] and was chosen for this reason; this example is not intended as a critique of the original work. Study 1 includes data from 253 participants, each completing 180 Stroop trials after each of the two tasks, and we use all of them.

```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE, tidy=FALSE}
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("mar-cald/multibayes")
library(multibayes); library(brms); library(dplyr)

stroop1 <- subset(afex::stroop, subset = study == 1)
data_stroop <- stroop1 |>
  # remove useless levels id
  dplyr::mutate(id = droplevels(pno)) |>
  # select relevant variables
  dplyr::select(id, condition, congruency, trialnum, acc, rt) |>
  group_by(id, condition) |>
  mutate(prev_cong = lag(congruency)) |> # previous cong
  ungroup() |>
  na.omit()
```

Given the repeated-measures structure of the data and the large number of trials per participant, we fit a multilevel generalized linear model using `brms` [@Paul2017] on reaction time (RT) data. A lognormal model was specified with the default flat priors. We used them because they are the most common choice in applied work and the one in which the penalty matters most, not as a recommendation.

The model includes the effects of congruency (congruent vs. incongruent), previous congruency (congruent vs. incongruent), condition (depletion vs. control), and trial (position within the 180 trials of a condition, standardized). The sequential congruency effect was modeled as the interaction between congruency and previous congruency. A possible effect of depletion was modeled through condition and its interactions with congruency and trial, so that depletion could change response times overall, change the congruency effect, or change how either evolves over the trials.

The question of the study is whether ego depletion affects performance, so the family consists of the four effects involving condition (@tbl-hypotheses). The remaining effects, such as the congruency effect, are estimated but enter no claim, so they are not part of the family. Before the data we had no reason to judge any of the four more likely than another to be positive or negative, so we treat them as exchangeable and apply the same $\bar{\pi}$ to all of them. The prior-odds rule then says which of the four effects can be claimed, each on its own. If several were claimed, each would have a posterior probability of at least $.975$ under every prior in $\Gamma$, so the expected proportion of claims with the wrong sign among them would be at most $.025$. The rule would not give the probability that all of them hold together, which the simultaneous band and the joint directional rule give. A family that also included the congruency effect, which is expected to be large and positive, would not be exchangeable.

We compute $pd$ as $\max\!\big(\Pr(\theta > 0 \mid y),\, \Pr(\theta < 0 \mid y)\big)$ for all hypotheses. When the direction of each parameter is specified in advance, the argument `direction` (`"greater"` or `"less"`, for each hypothesis) computes $pd$ as the posterior probability of the predicted direction, with the same threshold. The rule then corresponds to a single prior for each parameter, the member of $\Gamma$ most skeptical of the predicted direction, and $pd_{\text{adj}}$ is the posterior probability under that prior.

| **Hypothesis** | **$\theta_\text{null}$** |
|----|:--:|
| $H_1$: condition effect | 0 |
| $H_2$: congruency $\times$ condition interaction | 0 |
| $H_3$: condition $\times$ trial interaction | 0 |
| $H_4$: congruency $\times$ condition $\times$ trial interaction | 0 |

: Tested Hypotheses for Reaction Times {#tbl-hypotheses}

We removed trials without a response and, of the remaining trials, retained only correct trials preceded by a correct response (i.e., error and post-error trials were excluded), yielding `r format(nrow(mod_rt$data), big.mark = ",")` observations.

```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE, tidy=FALSE}
data_rt <- data_stroop |>
  group_by(id) |>
  # remove error and post error trials
  filter(acc == 1 & lag(acc, default = 1) == 1) |>
  ungroup()

# set contrast
contrasts(data_rt$congruency) <- contr.sum(2)/2
contrasts(data_rt$prev_cong) <- contr.sum(2)/2
contrasts(data_rt$condition) <- contr.sum(2)/2
# trial standardized (z-score)
data_rt$trial <- as.numeric(scale(data_rt$trialnum))

mod_rt <- brm(
  formula = rt ~ 1 + congruency * prev_cong +
    congruency * condition * trial +
    (1 + prev_cong + congruency * condition + trial * condition || id),
  family = lognormal(), data = data_rt,
  cores = 3, chains = 3, iter = 8000, seed = 1)
```

Since `pd.adjust()` computes $pd$ values automatically from a matrix of posterior draws, we extracted the draws of the four effects in the family and set $\bar{\pi} = .8$. Under the estimation prior, each direction of a parameter has prior probability $.5$; with $\bar{\pi} = .8$, we allow either direction of each parameter to have prior probability as high as $.8$, so a claim requires a Bayes factor four times larger than under the unadjusted rule. This is the reference value for a judgment that up to 80% of them could be null. It reflects skepticism about whether the depletion manipulation affects Stroop performance at all.

```{r, echo=TRUE}
draws_rt <- as.data.frame(mod_rt)
# the family: the four effects involving condition
par_names <- grep("^b_.*condition", colnames(draws_rt), value = TRUE)
draws_rt  <- draws_rt[, par_names]
pd.adjust(draws = draws_rt, pi.max = 0.8, null.value = 0)
```

```{r}
#| label: ex-counts
#| echo: false
ex   <- suppressWarnings(pd.adjust(draws = draws_rt, 
                                   pi.max = 0.8, null.value = 0))
EXc  <- attr(ex, "threshold"); EXcs <- attr(ex, "threshold.adj")
EXpd <- setNames(ex$pd, rownames(ex))
EXadj <- setNames(ex$pd.adj, rownames(ex))
EXn0 <- sum(EXpd >= EXc); EXn1 <- sum(EXpd >= EXcs)
num_word <- function(k) c("no", "one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six", "seven", "eight", "nine")[k + 1]
INT <- "b_congruency1:condition1"
# congruency effect (incongruent minus congruent, log RT) after each task;
# sum contrasts: congruent = +.5, control = +.5
fe <- brms::fixef(mod_rt)[, "Estimate"]
EXint_ctrl <- -(fe[["congruency1"]] + 0.5 * fe[["congruency1:condition1"]])
EXint_depl <- -(fe[["congruency1"]] - 0.5 * fe[["congruency1:condition1"]])
EXbelow <- names(EXadj)[EXadj < 0.5]
# joint directional statement and simultaneous band
EXj <- joint(draws_rt, interval = FALSE, null.value = 0)
EXb <- joint(draws_rt, interval = TRUE)
EXk <- sum(EXj$joint_cum >= 0.975)
band <- function(p, d) sprintf("[%.*f, %.*f]", d, EXb[p, "lower"], d, EXb[p, "upper"])
EXband <- rownames(EXb)[EXb$lower > 0 | EXb$upper < 0]
# the text below describes this pattern
stopifnot(EXn0 == 1, EXn1 == 1, EXpd[[INT]] >= EXcs, EXk == 1,
          identical(EXband, INT), fe[["congruency1:condition1"]] < 0,
          setequal(EXbelow, c("b_condition1:trial", "b_congruency1:condition1:trial")))
```

The printed header reports $m$, $\bar{\pi}$, the threshold $c$, and the value $c^*$ that $pd$ must reach. With the default $c = `r nz(EXc, 3)`$, a claim requires $pd_{\text{adj}} \geq `r nz(EXc, 3)`$, that is, $pd \geq `r nz(EXcs, 4)`$. Each row gives the posterior median, $pd$, and $pd_{\text{adj}}$ (`pd.adj`) of a parameter, and a short note below the table explains $pd_{\text{adj}}$.

Only the congruency $\times$ condition interaction (`b_congruency1:condition1`) has $pd \geq c$, with $pd = `r nz(EXpd[[INT]], 4)`$, and it also has $pd_{\text{adj}} = `r nz(EXadj[[INT]], 3)`$, at or above $c$. The claim therefore holds under every prior in $\Gamma$. On the log scale, the congruency effect, the difference between incongruent and congruent trials, was `r nz(EXint_ctrl, 3)` after the low-demand task and `r nz(EXint_depl, 3)` after the high-demand task, so the claim is that the congruency effect is smaller after the high-demand task. None of the other three effects reaches $c$, with or without the adjustment. For two of them, the condition $\times$ trial interaction ($pd = `r nz(EXpd[["b_condition1:trial"]], 3)`$, $pd_{\text{adj}} = `r nz(EXadj[["b_condition1:trial"]], 3)`$) and the three-way interaction ($pd = `r nz(EXpd[["b_congruency1:condition1:trial"]], 3)`$, $pd_{\text{adj}} = `r nz(EXadj[["b_congruency1:condition1:trial"]], 3)`$), $pd_{\text{adj}}$ is below $.5$, so the priors in $\Gamma$ disagree on which direction is more probable, and the data do not establish even a leaning in either direction.

The function `plot()` draws, for each parameter, the range of the posterior probability of its favored direction across $\Gamma$ (@fig-example):

```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE}
plot(pd.adjust(draws = draws_rt, pi.max = 0.8))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-example
#| fig-cap: "Posterior Probability of the Favored Direction Across the Class for the Four Effects Involving Condition"
#| apa-note: >
#|   Output of `plot()` for the worked example ($\bar{\pi} = .8$). Each bar spans the posterior probability of the favored direction across $\Gamma$, from $pd_{\text{adj}}$ (left end) to its value under the prior most favorable to that direction (right end); points mark $pd$, and the two ends of each range are printed on the right. The dashed line marks $c = .975$. Only the congruency $\times$ condition interaction lies entirely at or above $c$. Its range, from $.994$ to $.9996$, is shorter than its point, because close to 1 the priors in $\Gamma$ change the posterior probability very little. The bars of the condition $\times$ trial and three-way interactions cross $.5$.
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| crop: false
#| echo: false
par(cex = 1.1)
plot(ex)
```

A companion function, `joint()`, implements the simultaneous-band rule and the joint directional rule compared in the simulation study. By default, it returns simultaneous equal-tailed credible intervals:

```{r, echo=TRUE}
joint(draws_rt, prob = .95)
```

Only the band of the congruency $\times$ condition interaction ($`r band(INT, 4)`$) excludes 0, so the simultaneous-band rule makes the same single claim.

Setting `interval = FALSE` returns instead the joint posterior probability of the $k$ strongest directional claims, for each $k$:

```{r, echo=TRUE}
joint(draws_rt, interval = FALSE, null.value = 0)
```

The rows are sorted by decreasing $pd$, and `joint_cum` gives this probability for the first $k$ rows. Here it is $`r nz(EXj$joint_cum[1], 4)`$ for the strongest claim alone and $`r nz(EXj$joint_cum[2], 2)`$ for the two strongest, so the joint directional rule at $.975$ also accepts only the claim about the congruency $\times$ condition interaction. In this family, the three procedures agree.

# Discussion

The probability of direction ($pd$) is the posterior mass on the data-favored side of a reference point null value, equivalently, the larger of the two one-sided posterior probabilities. It is common practice to claim a direction whenever $pd$ exceeds a fixed threshold $c$, typically $.975$. Under an estimation prior symmetric about the null value, the direction selected after inspecting the data has the same prior probability as the opposite one, so each such data-selected hypothesis is evaluated at prior odds of one, and the rule $pd \geq c$ leaves these odds unchanged. With $m$ parameters that are independent a priori, the prior probability that every claim is false is then $.5^m$, whichever claims are made. The rule thus involves two separate choices, the posterior probability required to make a claim, $c$, and the prior odds of each direction, and neither takes the number of tests into account. Building on @Jeffreys1938 [see also @Westfall1997] and on Bayesian approaches to FDR control [@Scott2006; @Scott2010; @Guo2010; @Abraham2022; @Efron2001; @Storey2003; @Storey2002; @Stephens2017], the procedure presented here leaves $c$ unchanged and requires each claim to hold even when its prior odds are lowered, by an amount the researcher sets through a single quantity, $\bar{\pi}$, an upper bound on the prior probability of each direction of a parameter. A claim is then made when $pd_{\text{adj}}$, its posterior probability under the prior most skeptical of it, reaches $c$, which requires $pd$ to reach the larger value $c^*$. Every claim made therefore has a posterior probability of at least $c$ under every prior in $\Gamma$, so the expected proportion of claims with the wrong sign among those made is at most $1 - c$. The rule does not give the probability that all the claims hold together, which the joint directional rule and the simultaneous band give.

If the direction of a test is specified in advance, the rule reduces to a single prior for that parameter, the one that gives the predicted direction prior probability $1 - \bar{\pi}$. Whether or not the direction is specified in advance, the priors under which claims are evaluated are continuous and give point null effects no probability. Because the procedure evaluates only directional claims, not making a claim reflects the absence of a directional discovery, not evidence that the effect is null. Evaluating whether an effect is null requires other methods, such as those based on the two-group, or spike-and-slab, prior, which places probability exactly at the null value [@Scott2006; @Scott2010; @Stephens2017]. In Bayesian approaches to FDR control based on this prior, the proportion of null effects can be learned from the data [@Scott2010; @Stephens2017], but this requires large families [@Storey2002; @Efron2001], larger than those typical of psychological studies. 

The proposed adjustment keeps the researcher's continuous prior, so every claim is a statement about the sign of a parameter, and null effects enter only through the choice of $\bar{\pi}$. When the parameters in the family are exchangeable, $\bar{\pi}$ can be specified from a judgment about how many null effects the family could contain, instead of being learned from the data. In the simulations, a $\bar{\pi}$ matched to the proportion of null effects kept the FDR far below that of the unadjusted rule. The FDR increased gradually when $\bar{\pi}$ was below the proportion of null effects and decreased, at the cost of power, when it was above it. A researcher may also deliberately choose a $\bar{\pi}$ larger than the expected proportion of null effects, accepting this loss of power in exchange for fewer false claims.

The implementation applies directly to posterior draws or any posterior-derived $pd$. This raises the question of how to define the hypothesis family to which the correction applies [@Shaffer1995; @Hochberg1987]. Although no universal consensus exists regarding what constitutes a family, we favor the criteria proposed by @Westfall2011, where a family is a set of questions that *"form a natural and coherent unit, \[are\] considered simultaneously in the decision-making process, and/or present a set over which one plays pick-the-winner"*. Regardless of the chosen definition, authors should clearly specify their chosen family and explain how it serves the study's substantive goals.

We further recommend that researchers justify their choice of $\bar{\pi}$ by drawing on theory, expert elicitation, or domain expertise [@Hagan2019], and report this justification. Making this choice explicit serves two purposes. For researchers who use diffuse estimation priors, it states skepticism about the family without making the prior of any parameter narrower. For researchers who judge prior odds of one appropriate and decline the adjustment, it makes that commitment transparent.

A limitation is that applying the same $\bar{\pi}$ to every parameter assumes that they are exchangeable. In many models this is not the case; for example, a known main effect and an interaction term that motivated the study typically differ in prior plausibility. A common $\bar{\pi}$ set at the average proportion of null effects in the family is expected to keep the overall error rate close to that of an exchangeable family, since the rule applies the same threshold to every parameter, but it distributes errors unevenly. The threshold is too strict for the more plausible claims, which lose power, and too lenient for the less plausible ones, among which false claims are more frequent. In such cases the family can be divided into more homogeneous subsets, each with its own $\bar{\pi}$, or a conservative common value can be used. Parameters on which no claim is based need not be included in the family.

The derivation of the adjustment requires an estimation prior that is continuous and symmetric about the null value, because only then is $pd/(1 - pd)$ the Bayes factor [@Marsman2017]. Informative priors, such as a narrow normal prior centered on the null value, meet this condition, as do weakly informative and flat ones. The error rates and power reported here, however, were obtained in the normal model with a diffuse prior, and may differ in other models and with other priors.

If a minimum effect of practical interest $\delta$ can be specified, the question changes from the direction of an effect to whether it lies outside the region $(-\delta, \delta)$ [@Kruschke2018]. This hypothesis is fixed before the data, so the classical penalty applies to it directly. With a Cauchy prior of scale $\delta$, which places half its mass inside the region, the posterior odds equal the Bayes factor. Unlike the adjustment proposed here, this approach needs a proper prior chosen in light of $\delta$, and the direction of an effect outside the region is read from the posterior.

As Bayesian methods become increasingly common in psychological research, often with fixed decision thresholds, the implications of multiplicity should be explicitly recognized. The adjustment proposed here asks for one additional number, $\bar{\pi}$, and can be applied to the $pd$ values that researchers already report. We hope that claims based on $pd$ will be reported together with the family to which they belong, the value of $\bar{\pi}$ used, including $\bar{\pi} = .5$ when no adjustment is made, and the $pd$ and $pd_{\text{adj}}$ of every parameter in the family.
